title: Automated Inventory Image Processing for Boutique Retailers
business: A boutique fashion retailer that receives thousands of product photos daily from various suppliers, requiring immediate standardization and cataloging.
problem: The retailer previously relied on a dedicated server to resize and format images, which remained idle during off-peak hours while struggling to handle sudden spikes in inventory uploads during seasonal collection launches.
solution: By adopting serverless computing, the retailer replaces the static server with event-driven execution. When a supplier uploads a photo to cloud storage, an event triggers the execution of a function that processes the image. This ensures compute resources are only consumed during the actual transformation process, eliminating the need to manage server capacity or pay for idle time.
steps: Configure an event trigger on the cloud storage bucket to detect new file uploads.
Develop a function to handle image resizing, format conversion, and metadata extraction.
Deploy the function code to the serverless environment without provisioning underlying infrastructure.
Set appropriate execution permissions to allow the function to read from the source bucket and write to the catalog bucket.
outcome: The retailer achieves a seamless, scalable workflow where image processing capacity automatically adjusts to the volume of incoming files, ensuring consistent catalog updates without manual server oversight.
limitation: A primary limitation is the cold start latency, where the first execution after a period of inactivity may experience a slight delay as the environment initializes. Developers can monitor this by observing the initialization duration in execution logs to determine if provisioned concurrency is required for latency-sensitive tasks.

questions.question: In Automated Inventory Image Processing for Boutique Retailers, what is the primary benefit of using serverless computing over a dedicated server?
options: Eliminating the need to manage server capacity and paying only for consumed compute time.
Increasing the physical storage capacity of the boutique's local warehouse.
Reducing the total number of images that suppliers are allowed to upload.
Replacing all human staff with automated image processing algorithms.
questions.explanation: The scenario explains that serverless computing removes the need to manage servers and ensures costs are only incurred during actual execution, solving the problem of idle server costs.

When a supplier uploads a photo to cloud storage, an event triggers the execution of a function that processes the image. This ensures compute resources are only consumed during the actual transformation process, eliminating the need to manage server capacity or pay for idle time.

questions.question: In Automated Inventory Image Processing for Boutique Retailers, what is a potential trade-off of the serverless approach?
options: The system requires manual server patching every week.
Cold start latency may cause a slight delay for the first execution after inactivity.
The system cannot handle more than ten images per day.
The retailer must purchase additional hardware to support the event triggers.
questions.explanation: The limitation section explicitly identifies cold start latency as a trade-off inherent to serverless execution environments.
questions.evidence: A primary limitation is the cold start latency, where the first execution after a period of inactivity may experience a slight delay as the environment initializes.
